name: Ukraine

observations.reasoning: DISPUTED. Sourced on 2026-07-27, transversal pass over the population indicator. Population on 1 January 2022: 40997698 inhabitants, Eurostat dataset demo_pjan, read through the dissemination API. That is the last row Eurostat publishes for Ukraine, and the date is the whole problem: it is the stock recorded weeks before the full-scale invasion of February 2022. The status is disputed rather than verified because what is in question is not the figure, which is correctly read, but the denominator behind it. Total population of Ukraine in 2026 has no single answer: the resident population, the de jure population including those displaced abroad, and the population of territory under government control are three different numbers, and the indicator's denominator, written as simple total population, does not say which is meant. Recording 40.998 without that caveat would put a pre-war figure on a 2026 map. To be settled by a ruling on which population is counted, then sourced against a body that publishes on that basis.

Collected on 2026-07-28, in Ukrainian, in the transversal venues pass, and the count required two war rulings before it could be produced at all; both are written into schema.json. Twenty-four units, twenty-four houses, against an opening estimate of 22.5 produced with no research — the estimate was close and was close for the wrong reason, since it was a guess at a Soviet-legacy network and what is counted here is a network that has lost cities. The spine is first-party: UNIMA-Ukraine, the national centre, publishes a list of the state puppet theatres of the country, twenty-five of them, each with its own page carrying the legal title, the founding date, the direction and the contacts. That list is an enumeration of this denominator rather than a proxy for it: every entry is a standing institution whose vocation is puppetry, founded by an oblast or a city council and holding a building. Nineteen are regional, five are municipal — Dnipro, Kryvyi Rih, two in Kyiv and the marionette workshop — and one, Kharkiv, is on the state line. The oldest is Kyiv, 1927; Kharkiv counts its history from the All-Ukrainian Model Puppet Theatre founded in 1929; Zhytomyr is 1934, Vinnytsia 1937, Poltava 1938, Kropyvnytskyi and Zaporizhzhia 1939, Odesa 1932. Coordinates come from the OpenStreetMap gazetteer queried on each theatre's name, and where the gazetteer and the theatre's own history agree on a street the address is recorded — Zhytomyr on Mykhailivska 7 and Vinnytsia on Khmelnytske shose 7 are both the buildings their own pages describe. Two named institutions are deliberately not counted, and they are the reason this record took a ruling. The Kherson academic regional puppet theatre, founded in 1971 and housed at Universytetska 8, left the occupied city in May 2022 under threat, opened its 52nd season in Kolomyia and works there still: its rooms are lent to it by the Kolomyia academic Ukrainian theatre, Kolomyia having no puppet theatre of its own, and its building in Kherson was damaged again in November 2024. An institution working from premises another theatre lends it is a funded company without a venue while that lasts, which is the exclusion the denominator has carried since the beginning. The theatre is not diminished by that; the indicator is. It counts walls in use, and the war takes walls. The second is occupation. The Donetsk regional puppet theatre passed under the culture ministry of the self-proclaimed republic and took the word republican into its name, so its backing is no longer that of a public authority of Ukraine; it leaves this count and does not enter Russia's, because a seized institution is not evidence about the occupier's own field. Luhansk, Simferopol and Sevastopol are the same situation, read less well: the Ukrainian encyclopaedic entry for the Luhansk regional puppet theatre still gives its address on 16-Liniia and says nothing of what happened after 2014, and no current source was found. One further case falls on vocation rather than war. The Sumy theatre for children and young people was founded in 1974 as the oblast puppet theatre and reorganised in 1981; it calls itself the only theatre in Ukraine combining two arts, drama and puppetry, in one company, and names no puppet stage inside itself. That is the shape refused in Hungary for Kolibri and in Croatia for Osijek, and it is refused here for the same reason. The upper bound of 28 holds Kherson, Sumy, and the private field, which was not examined: UNIMA lists seven private puppet theatres beside the state ones, and a Ukrainian theatre blog's catalogue reaches some forty-nine companies of every form of ownership, of which at most a couple are likely to hold a hall. What has not been done, and is the first thing to open next, is a reading of the theatres' own repertoire and attendance: several of these houses publish season figures, which is the door to the performances indicator for a country whose statistical service has published nothing comparable since 2021.

One establishment retained: the Department of Puppet Theatre Art of the Karpenko-Kary national university of Kyiv, within the faculty of theatre arts. Criteria read at source: a department whose title names puppet theatre art explicitly, attached to a national and therefore state university. Caveat on record: the page read sets out the department's structure but does not enumerate its degrees; the bachelor's level in puppet theatre acting was seen only in a search summary, never at source. The degree-granting criterion is therefore presumed from the university attachment, not verified line by line. Upper bound at 2: the state academy of culture in Kharkiv was not checked in this pass.
